`strategy:sleep-scale-economies-shared` | confidence: **verified** | tags: global, india, process, quality, compounding

Model: a firm that passes its scale savings back to customers (lower prices, better service) grows volume faster, which deepens scale advantages, which allows more sharing - a flywheel competitors without scale cannot match. Costco (low fixed markups, membership fees) and Amazon (prices, free shipping, reinvestment) were Nomad's archetypes. Tools: (1) destination analysis - estimate what the business looks like in 10-20 years and whether today's price reflects it; (2) judge management by whether they sacrifice near-term margin for customer value; (3) concentrate in the best 3-10 ideas and hold through noise; (4) avoid 'scale economies kept' (firms raising prices on captive customers), which invites competition and regulation. Indian candidates for the test: discount retail, low-cost brokers/AMCs, platform businesses, airlines with cost leadership - but verify the customer-value claim with data (prices vs competitors, volume share).

Links: person:nick-sleep (about)

Sources: <https://quartr.com/insights/investment-strategy/investing-mastery-with-nick-sleep-nomad-s-costco-investment> ; <https://massivemoats.substack.com/p/a-deep-dive-analysis-into-the-nomad>

`insight:buffett-institutional-imperative` | confidence: verified | date: 1990-03-02

1989 letter, called his 'most surprising discovery': 'rationality frequently wilts when the institutional imperative comes into play.' Four forms, verbatim: '(1) As if governed by Newton's First Law of Motion, an institution will resist any change in its current direction; (2) Just as work expands to fill available time, corporate projects or acquisitions will materialize to soak up available funds; (3) Any business craving of the leader, however foolish, will be quickly supported by detailed rate-of-return and strategic studies prepared by his troops; and (4) The behavior of peer companies, whether they are expanding, acquiring, setting executive compensation or whatever, will be mindlessly imitated.' Cause is 'Institutional dynamics, not venality or stupidity'. The 1990 letter applies it to banks: lenders 'played follow-the-leader with lemming-like zeal; now they are experiencing a lemming-like fate', and at 20x assets/equity 'mistakes that involve only a small portion of assets can destroy a major portion of equity.' Berkshire's response: concentrate in companies 'alert to the problem'. Actionable checklist for Indian companies: cash pile growing + 'diversification' into unrelated areas (imperative #2); every peer announcing the same capex (#4, e.g., capacity waves in cement, steel, specialty chem, NBFC loan books); CEO pet projects with consultant decks (#3). Also: 'We've never succeeded in making a good deal with a bad person.'

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1989.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1990.html

body:
- **Precise vs vague.** Skipper: precise 33% < range 53% < vague 64%. KEC: 21% / 42% / 25%. KPIL: 72% / 65% / 75%. **Precise promises are not more reliable at any of the three.** Specificity raises a promise's weight but not its odds. The Skipper finding ("precise does worst") holds at KEC (precise is the worst bucket) but not at KPIL, where the buckets are flat. Keep the specificity weight (it measures how informative a promise is), but don't read precision as confidence.
- **Volunteered vs prompted.** Skipper: 39% vs 42% (no difference). KEC: 48% vs 22%. KPIL: 91% vs 58%. At two of three companies, **numbers volunteered in the prepared remarks are far more reliable than numbers given under analyst questioning.** KPIL publishes its guidance in the opening remarks every May; KEC almost never does (64 of 75 KEC promises were prompted). A useful screen is to ask whether the company states its guidance unprompted and repeats it.
- **Candour vs credibility run opposite ways here.** KEC has the highest candour index (31%: misses are explained in the opening remarks) and the lowest delivery. KPIL has the lowest candour (8%) and the highest delivery, but only 24 shortfalls, most of them minor. So candour is not a proxy for credibility. Read it as how a management behaves *after* a miss, and only compare it across companies with a similar number of misses.
- **Credibility decays with the cycle at the weaker two.** FY26-call promises delivered 20-25% at KEC and Skipper, against 53-56% for their FY25-call promises. KPIL barely moved (73% -> 67%). The ratio of FY26-call to FY25-call delivery is a cheap early signal: a management whose newer promises keep missing has not re-based to conditions.

Pre-registered India test (`research_notes/Allocation/allocation_test_india.md`, Apr-2006→Oct-2026, fund NAVs after fees, taxes and
costs): 100% equity 10.1%/yr, worst fall −55%, 70 months peak-to-peak; 70/20/10 equity/gold/bonds reset each January 10.9%/yr,
−38%, 21 months. New-money-to-underweight SIP (no selling, no tax) beat the yearly-reset SIP (11.3% vs 11.1% XIRR). P/E tilt did
NOT beat a fixed split at its own average weight → **rule: any timing rule must beat a fixed split at its average weight.**
Caveats: gold's 13.2%/yr includes 3.7%/yr rupee fall and a 72% jump in 2025; with gold capped at 7%/yr the split costs 0.4pp/yr but
still cuts the worst fall 16pp; the benefit is mostly 2008; equity still won 2/3 of 5-yr windows. Insurance, not extra return.
